## Growth-extract findings: PRs #971, #970, #969, #966, #963

Note: all five PRs show **zero review threads/comments** — solo-authored, auto-merged, no review discussion to mine. Lessons below come from diff + PR body only.

**#971 — Manual tasks refused their own forced items, so both fleet levers were dead**
Candidate lesson: *When a scheduler's dispatch mechanism changes how it treats forced/manual work (here: slot-bypass → queue-evaluates-precondition-at-pick), every task whose precondition assumed the old mechanism must be re-audited — a stale `run: false` that was previously "consulted by nothing" becomes a live self-closing landmine.* This is durable and non-obvious: the PR explicitly frames it as "the third instance of one class" (#929, #921, this one) and predicts a fourth (`fleet-digest`). Quote: *"Under the slot mechanism this said NO... The queue evaluates it at pick, and a manual task has no anchor to roll to — so a no-go would close the enforcer's own item `outcome:obsolete` without running."* Worth landing as a rule: after any scheduler-mechanism flip, grep for `frequency: 'manual'` + its precondition text, not just the mechanism's own callers.

**#970 — CI work-scope guard asserts the runner answers, not that the branch is clean**
Candidate lesson: *A unit test that invokes a real conformance/lint sweep and asserts the tree comes back clean will fail for any future legitimate finding — as a "broken test," at the wrong layer, one step before the actual gate that should report it.* Fix: assert only that the invocation is well-formed (exit 0 or 1, never a crash; a failing exit names what failed) and leave verdicts to the dedicated CI step. Quote: *"That makes any branch carrying a finding fail as a broken test — wrong layer, wrong message, and one step before the sweep that reports it properly."* This is a reusable test-layering principle (found via a probe PR #967 built specifically to catch it) and not yet stated in the local rules — a solid candidate.

**#969 — Bump every pack whose content was edited without a version bump**
No durable lesson found. This is a one-time mechanical backlog cleanup (29 packs) whose *going-forward* invariant is already fully enforced by the `pack-version-bumped` check landed in the preceding PR (#965). Nothing here explains a reason a check/test doesn't already cover.

**#966 — Run the work-scope sweep in CI, not only at a session's Stop hook**
Candidate lesson: *A diff-scoped CI check has a silent failure mode distinct from "wrong verdict" — an unresolvable base ref collapses the diff to empty, and an empty diff passes every rule with no output, indistinguishable from a genuinely clean sweep.* Two concrete, reusable habits: (1) `actions/checkout` leaves no local tracking ref for the base branch, so it must be fetched explicitly before diffing; (2) print the scope size and hard-fail on zero, because a silent tool can't tell you "judged nothing" from "judged clean." Quote: *"the first CI run of this step was green with no output at all, which proves neither"* and *"a work scope with no base resolves to an empty diff — which passes every rule, silently."* This is a strong, generalizable CI-authoring lesson (any diff/change-scoped gate in any repo), and was found the hard way (referenced by #939, needed a follow-up probe PR #967 to actually red it). Good candidate for `claudinite/RULES.md` or a portable CI-authoring note.

**#963 — Store the usage aggregates as declared counter tuples**
No new durable lesson found. The format-design writeup is detailed, but its one load-bearing principle — *"Unknown is not zero... decoding drops the key and the accumulator starts it from the first day that carries it"* — is already fully stated as an existing rule in `packs/basics/RULES.md` ("Handling a value that can be unknown — unknown is a state of its own: never encode it as a zero..."). This PR is an instance of that rule, not a new one.

## Summary
Two solid candidates worth writing up: **#971** (audit manual-task preconditions after any scheduler mechanism flip — recurring failure class) and **#966** (diff-scoped CI checks must guard against silent empty-diff-passes-everything, via explicit base fetch + non-empty-scope assertion). **#970** is a plausible but narrower test-layering lesson (arguably a specific case of the broader "test the mechanism not a moving target" idea) worth a short bullet if not already implied elsewhere. **#969** and **#963** yield nothing new — fully captured by an existing check or existing rule respectively.

{"number":977,"title":"Members' CI gates the change, not only the tree","body":"Closes #976. Follows [#966](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/966), which put the work sweep in the canon's own CI.

## The carrier decides the design

A member's `.github/workflows/` is member-owned and nothing converges it, so the standing rule applies: ask what carries a contract across the fleet before tightening one. What *does* converge, wholesale, on every converge, is the **engine tree** — so the recipe goes there and members carry an invocation that never changes.

**New: `engine/checks/ci-work-scope.mjs`** — the work scope's CI entry point, the counterpart to `check_the_world.mjs`. It owns the three things that separate a gate from a green light, each a way to look green while judging nothing:

| | why it exists |
|---|---|
| fetches the base ref | a CI checkout carries none, and a baseless work scope is an empty diff that passes every rule |
| refuses an empty scope | the runner is as silent about judging nothing as about a clean sweep |
| skips `claudinite/…` branches | the engine's own update/maintenance PRs have no session and no issue; their auto-merge is a queue for checks, so a red check there stops the repo updating rather than annoying anyone |

Every outcome prints why, and the runner's verdict becomes the exit code.

**The canon now runs that same entry point** — the inline bash #966 added is gone. Two spellings of one protocol in two trees is precisely the drift #801/#907/#929 were made of.

## What members get

- **`conformance-work-scope`** (core, **advisory**) — fires on a member whose CI gates the tree on every PR but runs no work sweep, with the one-line remedy. Advisory for the reason its sibling `conformance-workflow` is: a requirement added with no path to comply first is the #555 failure. Inert without a mount, and inert on a mount that predates the entry point — never a finding nobody can act on. A project that wires its sweeps into a `make` target or npm script satisfies it too.
- **bootstrap Part 8** now wires both sweeps (it previously said, in as many words, that only the world sweep belongs in CI), plus the `fetch-depth: 0` note the work sweep needs.
- **adopt-claudinite** follows.
- `core` bumped 3 → 4 so the pack actually ships — enforced now by `pack-version-bumped` from #965.

## Proof

`engine-tests/ci-work-scope.test.mjs` covers all four outcomes by **exit code and printed line**, including a fixture whose local pack always fires, proving a blocking finding reaches the exit code rather than being swallowed. `packs-tests/core/conformance-work-scope.test.mjs` covers the rule, including both inert cases; seen failing before it passed.

The first CI run went red on one test that passed locally: a fixture `git commit` spawned directly rather than through the test helper, which carries the `GIT_AUTHOR_*` identity a runner has no global config for. Reproduced locally with the identity removed, fixed by routing fixture git through the helper, and confirmed by running the pre-fix file under the same conditions.

Green on [run 32080000048](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32080000048), where the new entry point gated this very PR: `work scope: 10 changed file(s) vs origin/main`.

## Not in this PR

{"number":941,"title":"Task-owned trackers, and no fallback for a missing required input","body":"Rebased onto current `main`. Three commits.

## 1. A task's standing tracker is the task's own

Reworked after review — the earlier version made the tracker a machinery feature (a `tracker` title in the contract, resolved by the scheduler). Withdrawn. Two tasks already resolved a tracker in their **own** prework, each with a private copy of the same search, already diverged: one filtered `is:open`, which never matches a tracker at rest, so it would open a second one the moment anybody closed the first.

- `engine/scheduler/tracker.mjs` is a **library** a task's prework may call — exact-title lookup (re-filtered on equality, since `in:title` is a text match that returns siblings), the create-then-close pair ([#951](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/951)), the body/comment write. Nothing in the scheduler knows a task keeps one.
- **Creation is a separate call**, because whether a run with nothing to say should mint a tracker is the task's judgment — the answer [#953](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/953) just gave for the tidy trio is *no*.
- **A failed search throws** rather than reading as "no tracker exists" — otherwise a rate-limited search mints a fresh tracker every time it fails.

**The bug this uncovered:** both workers already passed their number on as `delivered: { issue: n }`, and **neither dispatch path rendered it**. `deliveredLines` handled only `pr` and `branch`, so the number reached no agent and the agentic phase searched by title anyway. Both paths now render an `Issue:` line, with a test each.

## 2. The postwork design record

Design only. No contract field, no executor change.

## 3. An agentic phase's required inputs are stated, and a missing one fails the run

An agentic phase has no `throw`, so the worker doc is the only thing that can supply the stop. Left unsaid, a missing input is an invitation to improvise — search the tracker by title, take the newest branch, enumerate the fleet — and each of those substitutes another run's inputs for this one's while the run still reports success.

- Every doc that reads a dispatch parameter (`ci-performance`, `growth-dedup`, `fleet-digest`) now names it **required** and says an absent one converges to `needs-human`, naming what was missing.
- Both executor briefs (`executor.md`, `queue/instructions.md`) carry the general form, so a task that adds a parameter later inherits it.
- The rule itself lands in the `unattended-agents` skill, as the prose twin of the existing fail-fast rule for orchestration scripts.
- `task-phase-discipline` read those stops as discretionary skips. It now exempts a stop that converges to `needs-human` — a failure is not a skip — and a new fixture pair proves it still flags a real skip in a doc that mentions the failure state elsewhere.

## Verification

`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2117 pass, 0 fail. Both check suites clean. The `task-phase-discipline` exemption and the `Issue:` rendering were each run against the unchanged code first and fail there. Pack versions bumped for `basics`, `core`, `grow_with_claudinite`, `sheepdog`.

{"number":975,"title":"Rewrite the task doc around what a task actually is","body":"Fixes #972.

`packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md` is what a session reads before writing or changing a task. It described the **slot** mechanism — now the legacy opt-out, since `dispatchMode` defaults to `queue` — and taught two wrong models along the way.

## What was wrong

**"A task is agentic work."** The doc led with a scheduler that "creates dispatch issues (`ready-for-agent`) for agentic work" and filed `agent_model: none` as a footnote. `engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs` runs prework in the drain job and, absent an agent request, closes the item right there: *"Prework did this run's work; no agent was needed."* A deterministic script running in Actions with no workflow file of its own is the ordinary shape of a task.

**"A task is a scheduled run."** The title said so, and the framing hung every task off the hourly cron. The tick only instantiates *recurring* items; items come equally from `create-work-item`, a `wake` dispatch, and another task's fan-out, and `manual` tasks are never instantiated by the tick at all.

The "the repo's **only** cron" sentence sat in the middle of that and read as the definition of a task.

## What changed

`packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md` → [`packs/core/tasks.md`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/github-pages-deploy-action-8l1dtr/packs/core/tasks.md), rewritten in the present tense:

- Opens on what a task is — a unit of the repo's own work, executed in the repo's Actions run — with the agentic phase and the recurring anchor each named as optional.
- Four roles (generator / executors / agents / janitor), and the tick-then-drain pair that holds latency at zero without depending on a label event.
- **The work step is code; the agent is the escalation** — including the prework-then-`CLAUDINITE_REQUEST_AGENT` shape and why the secrets story means a workflow that exists only to hold a secret is redundant.
- **Where an item comes from** — four origins, equal in standing, with `manual` explained rather than mentioned.
- The declaration contract, the precondition-is-the-only-decision-point rule with `exclusive`, the label vocabulary (including why `task:ready` is not bookkeeping), terminal exits, and suspend vs. dormancy.
- **The scheduler workflow** section keeps the one-cron invariant — still enforced by `engine/selftest.mjs`, unchanged — as what it is: a property of that workflow. The "make it a task, delete the workflow" rule lives there too, with the exception stated precisely as *what must be declared at the job level and the scheduler's jobs don't carry* (an `environment:`, an OIDC `id-token`).

Retired along the way, per the authoring rule against narrating a superseded practice: the slot vocabulary, "re-arming lost trigger events" as a janitor job, and the executor-as-label-fired-routine description.

`core/RULES.md` splits its one task rule in two, so the reader who wants a job to run in Actions — and would otherwise author a workflow — is caught by a rule keyed to what they are doing.

## Sweep

`scheduled-tasks.md` → `tasks.md` across 17 files, including the `doc:` field of four checks. `docs/per-project-scheduling/` is a historical record — link targets updated, content untouched. Also corrected: the `github-actions-scheduling` skill's closing paragraph, which described the retired due-slot-against-the-run-ledger math; `packs/core/README.md`'s rule index and its `02:00 slot` → `02:00 anchor`; the concept name at four other reference sites.

Version bumped on `core`, `github-actions`, `product-wiki`, `sheepdog`.

## Verification

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2099 pass, 0 fail.
- `node engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs --changed --base origin/main` — exit 0.

Both failed first (`rule-index` on the added rule, `pack-version-bumped` on four packs) and were fixed rather than worked around.

## One thing I assumed

You called the "only cron" line annoying. I read that as the *framing* — it was being used to define a task — not as a request to allow a second cron, so the invariant and its selftest are untouched and the sentence now appears once, in the scheduler-workflow section. **Candidate lesson:** When sweeping references to a renamed/retired entity, recompute any golden test value that derives from the old name (rather than guessing the new one), and deliberately leave dated historical records unrenamed, distinguishing "same thing renamed" from "separate thing retiring."

Quote (PR body): *"The `hashedMinute` golden moves with its input — `missingbulb/Shepherd` hashes to **11**, computed from the live function, not guessed."* and *"`docs/per-project-scheduling/MIGRATION.md` Phase 3 repo list — a dated rollout record... naming Shepherd there would falsify the record."* This wasn't a rename (Sheepdog is retiring, Shepherd is a new repo), and the PR explicitly separated "live reference, must move" from "historical record, must stay" — a distinction worth generalizing beyond this one sweep.

## #935 — claudinite-dashboard pack (opt-in fleet/repo scheduler dashboard)
**Candidate lesson:** `.github/workflows/` is the one directory a repo's own automated nightly-update mechanism can never write to (its `GITHUB_TOKEN` is refused there), so anything needing a workflow file must arrive by being *seeded* at an adoption/install moment (a human- or session-held credential), not by ordinary convergence — and the corollary design split of freezing only the seeded shim while the logic it calls keeps converging out of the mount.

Quote (PR body): *"**`.github/workflows/` is the one directory the nightly update can never push to** — the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` is refused there. So a deploy workflow can only arrive by being *seeded*... That's why adoption is the wiring moment rather than a convergence."* This is a non-obvious platform constraint driving a real architectural choice (seeded stub vs. convergent code), not merely a fact about this one pack — worth capturing as a durable rule for any future pack needing a workflow file. No review discussion to corroborate/contest it (self-merged, zero threads), but the reasoning is checkable and specific enough to stand on its own.

## #938 — Unfreeze the fleet: accept legacy value-set spelling + mint standing item on force
**Candidate lesson:** Tightening a validated vocabulary/spelling that both the engine and a member's *vendored* packs must agree on can create a circular block — the PR that would deliver the fix gets parked by the very validation it introduces, because the engine ships every commit while packs ship only on a version bump, so a renamed key can reach the engine's rejection logic before it reaches any member's packs.

Quote (PR body): *"the mixed tree fails the self-test on `pack-manifests`, so `deliveryDecision` **parks the update PR**... that parked PR is the one that would have carried the new spelling... The secondary fix (mint a standing item when forcing finds none, since "for most of a daily task's day there is nothing to wake") is real but narrower/more mechanism-specific to this repo's own scheduler engine — plausibly already covered by this repo's existing "Wanting to exercise a task Action-side" / "Converging an unattended run" rules, so weaker as a *new* lesson.

{"number":976,"title":"Members' CI gates the tree but not the change","body":"Follows #939 and #966, which put the work-scope sweep into the **canon's** CI. Every member still gates only the world scope.

The two scopes answer different questions, and the tree sweep cannot stand in for the other: a version number is always present in `pack.mjs`, so only the diff says whether *this* change moved it. Same shape for every commit-scoped rule — the issue reference, an introduced merge commit, a contract change that owes a migration. Until now the work scope ran at a session's Stop hook and nowhere else, so it was enforced where a session happened to be: an unattended commit, a hand-pushed branch, or a hook that never fired reached `main` unjudged.

## What a member needs

One step beside the world sweep. The recipe must **not** be copied into every member's workflow — three parts of it are the difference between a gate and a green light, and all three want to converge centrally:

- **the base ref** — a CI checkout carries none, and a work scope with no base is an empty diff that passes every rule silently;
- **an empty scope** — the runner is as silent about judging nothing as about a clean sweep;
- **the `claudinite/…` skip** — the engine's own update and maintenance PRs have no session and no issue behind them, and their auto-merge is a queue for checks, so a red check there does not annoy anyone: it stops the repo updating, quietly and permanently.

So the logic lives in the engine tree (which vendors wholesale on every converge) as `engine/checks/ci-work-scope.mjs`, and a member carries only the invocation.

## Delivery

Advisory check (`conformance-work-scope`, core), so no member turns red on its next update — the same staging the world-scope rule used. Bootstrap Part 8 and the adoption skill wire both sweeps for new adoptions; existing members get the advisory finding with the one-line remedy.

{"number":974,"title":"Retire the slot scheduler: delete run.mjs, the slot half of slots.mjs, the slot stub and FORCE_TASKS","body":"The last item of #801 Step 3. Every member is on the queue and converged, so nothing in the slot mechanism is reachable any more — except through the callers listed below, which are the actual work.

Deliberately not started until #971 landed, because three of these callers were still live defects rather than dead code.

## Precondition (met)

All 12 adopted repos run the queue stub and have converged onto current canon. Deleting `run.mjs` strands any member whose workflow still calls it; none does.

## What actually dies

- `engine/scheduler/run.mjs` (636 lines) — the slot scheduler entry point
- `engine/scheduler/slots.mjs` — **only its slot half**: `dueSlots`, `FIRST_RUN_FREQUENCIES`, and the slot-id strings inside `mostRecentSlot`
- `engine/scheduler/stubs/claudinite-scheduler.yml` (94 lines) — the slot stub, and with it the `overrides` dispatch input
- `engine/scheduler/run-record.mjs`'s run-ledger half (`renderTaskRuns`, the watermark math)
- the slot-conformance checks in `packs/core/declared-checks.json`
- ~1,900 lines of slot-only tests (`run.test.mjs`, `slots.test.mjs`, `resolve-dispatch.test.mjs`, `run-record.test.mjs`, `signal-context.test.mjs`, `dispatch.test.mjs`)

## What must move first — this is not an `rm`

Four things the queue and the packs still genuinely need live inside the modules being deleted:

| what | lives in | needed by |
|---|---|---|
| `FREQUENCIES`, `DEFAULT_SCHEDULE`, `WEEKDAYS`, `normalizeSchedule`, the anchor arithmetic | `slots.mjs` | `queue/anchors.mjs`, `task-contract.mjs`, `packs/core/task-declaration-shape.mjs` |
| `buildSignalContext` | `run.mjs:313` | `queue/signals.mjs` |
| `ensureLabels` | `run.mjs` | `packs/basics/tasks/task-janitor/worker.mjs` |
| `parseOverrides` | `run.mjs` | `packs/sheepdog/tasks/fleet-digest/worker.mjs` |

Most of `slots.mjs` is calendar arithmetic with no slot identity in it. Suggested shape: rename `slots.mjs` → `calendar.mjs` carrying the frequency vocabulary and anchor instants (no ids), `buildSignalContext` → `signals/`, `ensureLabels` → `github.mjs`. Doing the extraction as a *separate earlier PR* would create a duplication window against the still-live `run.mjs`, so extraction and deletion belong in **one** change.

## The parameter plumbing — the real work

Four tasks take operator parameters through `CLAUDINITE_OVERRIDES`, the slot-era override bag:

- `sheepdog/fleet-baseline` — `REPOS`, `DRY_RUN`, `INCLUDE_DORMANT`
- `sheepdog/fleet-add-missing-packs` — `REPOS`, `ADD_PACKS`, `PACK_CONFIG`, `SCAN_FOR_NEEDED_PACKS`
- `sheepdog/fleet-digest` — `DIGEST_BACKFILL_DAYS`
- `core/adopt-requested-packs`

Under the queue, parameters ride the **item's Context**, and that path already exists: `prework-run.mjs` passes `CLAUDINITE_CONTEXT`. So each becomes a `create-work-item / --context "REPOS=…"`, and the workers swap which env var they parse — the `KEY=value` bag parser itself is unchanged, and `fleet-baseline`'s copy is already pack-local.

`fleet-digest` is the one to watch: merged in #958 *during* this migration, it added a fresh `parseOverrides` import from `run.mjs` and documents `FORCE_TASKS=fleet-digest` as its manual trigger. New slot-era callers are still arriving because the slot idiom is still the documented one, which is an argument for doing this soon rather than letting the surface grow again.

## Expect more of one class

Three defects so far were all "the flip changed a contract and its callers weren't swept":

| # | contract changed | caller left behind |
|---|---|---|
| #929 | the dispatch interface | Shepherd's fan-out tasks, sending `overrides` |
| #921 | the force recipe | DESIGN §8's own prose, omitting `task:ready` |
| #971 | forcing no longer bypasses the precondition | every `manual` task's precondition |

All three were invisible to Step 2's validation burst for the same structural reason: the burst exercised the queue's own paths, and each of these is a slot-era caller of a queue-era contract. Sweep for callers **outside** the module before deleting, and prefer a generic guard over a point fix each time one turns up — #971's guard quantifies over every declared task rather than naming the two that were broken.

## Done means

- [ ] the four helpers rehomed and their importers updated
- [ ] the four tasks take parameters via Context, with `FORCE_TASKS` gone from their docs and preconditions
- [ ] `run.mjs`, the slot half of `slots.mjs`, the slot stub, the ledger math and the slot-conformance checks deleted
- [ ] `grep -rn FORCE_TASKS` returns only historical citations (migration records, dated design docs)
- [ ] a forced `fleet-baseline` run observed converging a member end to end — the lever this whole thread exists to restore

So `parseOverrideBag` always returns `{}`, and therefore:

- `REPOS` — **dead**. No filter is possible; every run is the whole fleet.
- `DRY_RUN` — **dead**. Every run is live.
- `INCLUDE_DORMANT` — dead (fails safe: dormant members stay skipped).

The lever is runnable as of #971 but **only in its most dangerous mode**: unscoped and live. Its two safety knobs are silently inert, which is worse than absent — the operator can pass `DRY_RUN=true` in a Context line, see it accepted, and get a live fleet-wide sweep.

`fleet-add-missing-packs` has the same shape with more parameters (`ADD_PACKS`, `PACK_CONFIG`), where a silently-ignored `REPOS` means adopting packs into repos nobody named.

**Consequence for sequencing:** the Context plumbing should land *before* the first live `fleet-baseline` run, not after. That reorders this issue's own "done means" — the end-to-end observation of the lever depends on the plumbing rather than merely following it.

{"number":940,"title":"Task postwork: a deterministic phase after the agent","body":"A task run has a deterministic phase **before** the agent (`prework`) and nothing after it. Everything past the agent's judgment — landing the PR, reconciling the standing tracker, pruning logs — is prose the agent performs by hand over MCP, in every task, separately.

The survey that prompted this (2026-08-17) found four deterministic tails:

1. **PR delivery.** `engine/scheduler/land-pr.mjs` carries a hand-maintained prose twin, `engine/scheduler/deliver-pr.md`, whose header says the two must keep saying the same thing. That duplication exists only because an agent cannot run the module and there is no post-agent code phase. ~8 agentic tasks re-perform it.
2. **Tracker reconcile.** `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, `rule-revalidation`, `ci-performance`, `wiki-growth` each spell out the same find-by-exact-title / create-closed-if-absent / rewrite-body / dated-comment / never-open-or-close procedure. `tidy-issues` calls it "mechanical aggregation" in its own model note.
3. **`growth-extract`'s retention pruning** of `conversation-logs` — pure code, currently agentic work on an orphan branch, which is why the task doc has to forbid merges and history rewrites.
4. **Post-hoc outcome verification** — tracking-issue reference in the commit, write-scope, the `expected_outcome` ceiling — currently CI checks on a PR that already exists.

The split is not task-by-task: it is **judgment vs. the bookkeeping that records it**. Today one agent does both, so a run that exhausts its budget mid-bookkeeping leaves half a rewritten tracker.

**Scope of this issue (owner, 2026-08-17): the design record only** — `docs/task-postwork/DESIGN.md`, the mechanism. No contract fields, no executor change, no task converted. The open design question is the agent→code channel: prework's rule is "communicates only through the repository", and postwork needs the reverse direction.

Status, phases and remaining work are tracked here, not in the record.

{"number":972,"title":"core/scheduled-tasks.md teaches a stale task model — agentic-only, cron-defined","body":"## The problem

`packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md` is the doc every session reads before writing or changing a task (`core/RULES.md`). It still describes the **slot** mechanism, which is now the legacy opt-out — `dispatchMode` in `engine/scheduler/converge-wiring.mjs` defaults to `queue`. Two wrong models come out of it, both confirmed against a live session:

**1. "A task is agentic work."** The doc opens with a scheduler that "creates dispatch issues (`ready-for-agent`) for agentic work", and treats `agent_model: none` as a footnote exception. The engine says the opposite: `engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs` runs prework in the drain job and, when no agent is requested, **closes the item right there** — `Prework did this run's work; no agent was needed.` A task is deterministic code by default with an *optional* agentic phase. A task that runs a script in GitHub Actions with no dedicated workflow file is the ordinary shape, not a special case.

**2. "A task is a scheduled run."** The title says "Scheduled tasks"; the framing hangs every task off the hourly cron. Under the queue, the cron only drives the tick's *instantiation* of recurring items. Items are equally created by hand (`create-work-item`), by other tasks, by fan-out, and by a `wake` dispatch input; `manual` tasks are never instantiated by the tick at all (DESIGN §8). Scheduling is one origin among several.

The "the repo's **only** cron" sentence lands in the middle of this and gets read as the *definition* of a task rather than as what it is — a property of the scheduler workflow.

## Also stale in the same doc

- The three-responsibility split (scheduler / executor / janitor) — the queue refines this to four roles, and the scheduler's half that evaluated preconditions has moved into the executor.
- "re-arming lost trigger events" as a janitor job — the post-tick drain retires the re-arm.
- The executor described as "a per-repo routine fired by the label event" — it is a pull worker, and the drain is what keeps common-case latency at zero.

## The ask

Rewrite the doc around the current model, keep the one-cron invariant where it belongs (a scheduler-workflow property, still enforced by `engine/selftest.mjs`), and sweep the references. Historical design records under `docs/` are a record of their moment — links only, no content rewrites.

{"number":801,"title":"Migration to the work-item queue: two PRs, one same-day validation burst","body":"The phase plan for [tasks-dispatch DESIGN](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md) (§14 points here). Design constraints from the owner (2026-08-13): **fewest disparate steps, fewest approval points, and certainty the same day** — we do not wait for a nightly run to learn whether the end state works. Deliberately generating real work to push traffic through every path is explicitly sanctioned.

**Approval points: two.** PR‑1 (mechanism + canon flip) and PR‑2 (fleet flip + slot deletion). Everything else is forcing and observing, which the mechanism itself defines as ordinary operations.

Checkboxes track progress; each burst row's checkbox is checked only with an evidence URL appended beside it.

---

## Where this stands (2026-08-16 12:10Z)

**One member is verified end to end, agentic lane included. Twelve more are blocked on owner-only credential work.** Steps 0–2 complete. Step 3 is most of the way: the flip is merged and observed, the first member ran a real agentic item to `outcome:done`, and three defects the burst could not have caught were found and two fixed. The slot deletion still waits on the remaining members.

| | state |
|---|---|
| Canon | on the queue since #854; 12 clean scheduler runs overnight, 12 items to terminal state |
| Fleet | flipped by default in #888 (`17902b9`); **GCEC verified end to end**, 12 members still need a CCR routine (#916) |
| Slot machinery | still in the tree, deliberately — deleting it before members are verified strands them (see Step 3) |
| Design vs engine | DESIGN/sim current to §15.24 plus F24; engine at pre-review behavior — the catch-up is Step 4 (#883) |
| Open follow-ups | #916 (owner-only, blocking), #921, #892, #924, #883, #877 |

## Step 0 — rehearsal (done)

- [x] Simulator + scenario suite green in CI; coverage map names the live-only rows

## Step 1 — PR‑1 on canon: the whole mechanism, canon flipped (approval №1)

- [x] Label vocabulary, tick workflow (cron + `workflow_dispatch`), executor workflow, janitor re-target, dependency fields + `after` yield + `create-work-item`, F8 signal exclusions, canon flipped, gate green
- [x] **Approval №1: PR‑1 merged** — #854, `b30ef77`

## Step 2 — the validation burst (complete)

- [x] **B1 creation + first-item rule (S25):** [run 31899008771](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/31899008771) — 12 items #860–#870, each `task:blocked` wearing its next anchor
- [x] **B2 the roll + reasons on record (S1′):** #860 — one ask, rolled to tomorrow, reason on the item, no comment spam
- [x] **B3 agentic happy path + real CCR invocation + records (S2):** #867 — wake → claim → hand-off with nonce → **live session in 31s** → result + exec record → `outcome:done`
- [x] **B4 agentless path end to end:** #859 — wake → executor in 2s → claim → prework → `outcome:done`, closed in 26s, no session
- [x] **B5 the chain + yield (S4/S23):** #863 — yielded while `core/update` was live ([run 31913047785](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/31913047785)), then claimed and running the moment the upstream cleared; its work merged as #887
- [x] ~~**B6 hourly cadence**~~ — **dropped** (owner). `create-extractor` is `gcec/create-extractor` on GoogleCalendarEventCreator, the fleet's only hourly task; canon has none
- [x] ~~**B7 missing-secret posture**~~ — **folded into Step 3** (owner): every member reaches the flip with its endpoint token unset, so the posture happens on real traffic with no scaffolding
- [x] **B8 force-while-executing mutex (S15):** #871 — queued behind the executing twin, then got its own verdict on release
- [x] **B9 multi-executor lease (S7):** #873 — three overlapping executors, exactly one claim, one execution
- [x] **B10 follow-up fields (S17):** #872 — `Blocked-by` + `Not-before` created and held blocked by the tick
- [x] **B11 janitor leashes:** [run 31900490000](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/31900490000) — 12 blocked/rolling items, zero escalations
- [x] **All burst rows green**

### What the burst caught that the rehearsal could not

Four defects, none of which any simulator would have produced. Three are fixed:

- **#879 → #881 (merged).** Hand-off appended a second `### Context` instead of replacing the first, splitting the item's binding scope while `instructions.md` says to read "the Context section", singular. Every unit test passed, because each tested one call. Confirmed fixed on live traffic in B5's own hand-off.
- **#882 → #885 (merged).** Queue sessions wrote `[unknown]` where the exec record's slot id used to go — `instructions.md` never said what replaces it — dropping the join from a record back to its work item.
- **The task-path guard fired correctly** on a hand-built item naming `task.mjs` instead of `task.md` (#871): refused, converged to `needs-human`, nothing run.
- **#892 (open).** The terminal convergence is agent-discretion, and **both** agentic runs got part of it wrong — #867's record field, and #863 closing with no outcome label and no exec record at all. Proposes a `converge-item.mjs` the session calls with its judged outcome.

## Step 3 — the fleet flip, then the deletion (approval №2)

**PR‑2 is two PRs, not one** (amendment, 2026-08-15). The plan said "slot machinery deleted in this same PR"; that is unsafe, and the reason is in the code:

- `updates/engine-update.mjs` **replaces the mount wholesale**, so a file canon deletes leaves every member's mount on its next converge whatever that member's config says.
- `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot push — staged, and landed later by the apply stage.
- The two stubs call **different entry points**: `run.mjs` vs `queue/tick.mjs`.

So deleting slots in the flip's own release strands any member whose workflow has not yet landed. Keeping the slot code makes that window benign (`run.mjs` no-ops) and #888 makes it **loud**.

- [x] The pack update flow staged only the scheduler workflow, so `claudinite-executor.yml` reached no member — #874, `5ca4c35`
- [x] **Approval №2: the flip merged** — #888, `17902b9`. `dispatchMode` answers `queue` for an absent setting, so members flip with **no edit to any file they own**
- [x] **A member's converge observed** — GoogleCalendarEventCreator, 2026-08-16 02:00:18–02:00:25Z: both stubs call the queue entry points out of the mount, `taskScheduler` carries no `dispatch` key, mount `queue/tick.mjs` byte-identical to canon HEAD, and [15 standing items created](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/918) (GCEC #904–#918). Last slot-era item was GCEC #903 at 00:09Z
- [x] **B7 lands here** — and the fault was **not** the unset secret the plan anticipated. `resolveEndpoint` fails at the *declaration*: [GCEC #908](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/908#issuecomment-5305803329) parked `needs-human` naming `taskScheduler.endpoints`, no session started. `endpoints` was declared in exactly one repo in the fleet — this one — so the flip left **every** member's agentic lane dark
- [x] **Per-member mini-burst on the first member (B1–B4 + B7 + B3 agentic)** — GCEC: agentless lane ran clean from 02:00Z; [GCEC #908 closed `outcome:done` at 11:28:16Z](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/908) via a live session started 11:16:12Z, its work landing as GCEC #923; [GCEC #907 `core/update`](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/907) closed `outcome:done` 11:49:02Z, converging the mount through the queue itself
- [ ] **The other 12 members wired and observed** — blocked on #916 (owner-only: one CCR routine + `CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN` per repo)
- [ ] #921 folded in — DESIGN §8's force recipe yields an item `pickOrder` can never pick
- [ ] **Then** the slot deletion PR (slots.mjs, run-ledger math, exclusive claim, re-arm, `FORCE_TASKS` path, slot-conformance checks)
- [ ] The migration reports itself through the mechanism it ships: per-member fan-out items + a fan-in item `Blocked-by` all of them (S18 live) — fan-in closed `outcome:done`

### What Step 3 caught that Step 2 could not

Three defects, each invisible to the burst for a specific reason — and the reasons are the finding:

- **#906 → #907 (merged).** `queue/instructions.md` was never in the vendor set: `computeVendorSet` drops every `engine/**/*.md` behind a two-entry operational whitelist, and #854 added a third operational doc without extending it. That file *is* the behavior of a work-item session. **Invisible because canon runs the engine from its repo root, not a mount** — so no amount of canon traffic could show it.
- **#922 → #925 (merged).** F18's episode boundary was stated semantically and implemented over only the paths that already wrote a comment; the roll and the `needs-human` park end an episode silently, leaving a claim that outranks every future claimant. The roll self-heals via the leash (canon #860 sat unrunnable 17:44Z→03:32Z); the park never does. Fixed by *striking* the claim — including on the **losing** claimant, whose claim would otherwise become the earliest of the next episode. **Invisible because the simulator modelled the rule's intent rather than its artifact**, so it was correct by construction; the sim now models the artifact and reproduces the bug without the fix.
- **#921 (open).** DESIGN §8's force recipe — strip `task:blocked`, optionally add `task:urgent` — omits `task:ready`, and `pickOrder` admits on `task:ready` alone. A forced item is invisible to every executor and the run logs `nothing ready to pick up`, which looks exactly like a healthy run. **Invisible because no executable artifact pins DESIGN's prose recipes.**

## Step 4 — the work-as-work engine catch-up (#883; starts only after Step 3's verification)

#884 (merged 2026-08-16, `4380639`) changed the design under the shipped mechanism — decisions §15.14–24. **The behavior-by-behavior checklist lives in #883** — one box per capability, each stating what breaks while it's off; this plan owns only the sequencing:

- [ ] **Step 4 waits for Step 3's per-member verification** — the flip wave must be observed on the engine it shipped, not one changing underneath it
- [ ] Each #883 behavior lands burst-style per this plan's own discipline: a forced run observed on canon the same day; the workflow-touching pieces (heartbeat, decoupling, continuation job, suspend-all) additionally observed on one member's converge before the fleet's
- [ ] #892's `converge-item.mjs` is the natural carrier for #883's durable-record box — land them together, not twice
- [ ] #924 (a losing claimant's comment defers the leash reclaim) rides #883's heartbeat, which introduces the per-holder liveness signal it needs
- [ ] #877 (the tick rename) unblocks when this step closes — last, so the rename never churns files mid-migration

## Done means

- [x] All Step‑2 rows have evidence URLs on this issue
- [x] The first member flipped, wired and observed end to end — agentless and agentic
- [ ] All members flipped and observed; fan-in item closed `outcome:done`
- [ ] Slot machinery gone from the tree
- [ ] Step 4: the fielded engine matches DESIGN §15.14–24 — #883 closed
- [ ] 48h of ordinary operation as *confirmation* — explicitly not the proof; the burst was the proof

Two changes to the design landed inside PR‑1 and are worth naming here, because both simplify what Step 2 has to prove:

- **Invocation is a routine's API trigger**, verified against the routines docs rather than assumed. Firing a routine runs *its stored prompt*, and our `text` arrives wrapped as untrusted — so the payload names the item and the nonce and instructs nothing, and the session's instructions are a tracked file (`engine/scheduler/queue/instructions.md`) that the routine's one-line prompt points at.
- **One call per item, never retried** (owner correction) — which deleted the agent-side claim protocol rather than simplifying it. There is no idempotency key on the endpoint, so a retry is precisely how two sessions land on one item. An unanswered call now leaves the item with the agent, and the janitor's agent leash settles it either way. `MAX_HANDOFF_ATTEMPTS`, the attempt counter and the bounded revert are all gone.

The flip half is ready. The **slot deletion cannot ride with it**, and the reason is in the code rather than the plan:

- `updates/engine-update.mjs` **replaces the mount wholesale** (`rmSync` + re-copy), so a file canon deletes leaves every member's mount on its next converge regardless of that member's config.
- `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot push — the engine flow runs `workflows: false`, `env: {}`, and the content is staged for the apply stage.
- The two stubs call **different entry points**: `run.mjs` vs `queue/tick.mjs`.

So deleting slots in the same release strands any member whose workflow has not yet been landed: its hourly cron runs a file the mount no longer has, and the apply stage that would fix it is work the dead scheduler dispatches. Non-self-healing, and the same shape as the #651/#652 wedge.

Keeping the slot code makes that window benign (`run.mjs` no-ops) — and #888 makes it **loud**, since reaching that branch at all proves the workflow is still the slot shim.

**Proposed amendment to this plan:** PR‑2 becomes two PRs — the flip (#888), then deletion once every member is confirmed on the queue. Same day, so no-lingering-legacy still holds; just not in an order that can strand a member. The Step 3 checklist above reads as one PR and should be read as two.

[{"id":5316661692,"body":"Two more findings from the same adoption, on the owner's instruction to keep them here rather than open separate issues. Both are about **how a human-handover step is written**, so they sit one level up from the path bug above — that one is a wrong address, these are a wrong shape.

## 1. A GitHub settings step must be a deep link, not a breadcrumb trail

The handover issue this adoption produced said things like:

> Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret

Every one of those is a URL the agent already knows how to construct — it has the `owner/repo` — so making the human navigate is pure friction, and a breadcrumb goes stale the moment GitHub reorganizes a settings page while a URL keeps redirecting. The rule the owner asked for: **hyperlink every requested GitHub setting change, to the deepest page that exists.**

The patterns worth naming wherever this lands:

| Step | URL |
|---|---|
| New Actions secret | `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/settings/secrets/actions/new` |
| Actions secrets and variables | `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/settings/secrets/actions` |
| Workflow permissions, Actions general | `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/settings/actions` |
| Auto-merge, merge methods, general | `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/settings` |
| Branch protection / rulesets | `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/settings/branches` |
| Environments | `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/settings/environments` |

This is general to every repo the fleet adopts, not specific to the one that hit it — which is why it is here and not in that repo's local pack.

## 2. Don't ask a human to enable something GitHub enables by default

The same issue carried a checkbox for **Settings → General → "Allow squash merging"**, on the reasoning that the merge recipe squashes always. But GitHub enables all three merge methods on a new repository, so the box could only ever be already-ticked. A handover list whose items are mostly no-ops teaches the reader to skim it, which is exactly the failure mode a handover list exists to prevent.

Worth stating as a rule where the handover shape is defined: **a handover step must name a change from the platform's default.** If the default already satisfies the requirement, the requirement is met and there is nothing to hand over.

Both corrections are applied in the consuming repo's own issue ([missingbulb/Shepherd#3](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/3)) — this is the upstream half, so the next adoption does not repeat either.

One consequence of keeping all three here: this issue's title now names only the first finding. Worth retitling to something like *"bootstrap.md Part 9 path bug, plus two rules for writing human-handover steps"* if it is going to be triaged by title.

{"number":939,"title":"Pack content ships on a version bump but the engine validating it ships regardless — the asymmetry froze the whole fleet for five days","body":"Found while forcing TLDR to converge for #801. The immediate unblock is in #938's branch; **this issue is the cause, which that change deliberately does not fix.**

## What happened

Every member repo has been stuck on canon ref `631a067f` since **2026-08-12**, receiving nothing at all — not #907, not #925, not #936.

| repo | `instructions.md` in mount | stamped ref |
|---|---|---|
| TLDR, LaughCounter, CrosswordChat, Sheepdog, EdFringeNow, VascularColoring, ShoutsAndWhispers | ❌ | `631a067f` |
| ClaudiniteCanary | ❌ | `e3e0a919` |
| GoogleCalendarEventCreator | ✅ | `631a067f` |

GCEC is the only exception and not a real one — that file is there because it was written by hand.

## Why it could not self-heal

1. #895/#908 replaced the inline `eachValueInParsedArray` quantifier with `eachValueOfSet` + a named `extractValueSets` entry, updating canon's own packs in the same commit — so **canon CI stayed green**.
2. A member's vendored **packs** are delivered on a **pack version bump**. `chrome-extension-release` is still `version: 1`, and members have `1` stamped — so the new spelling reached **nobody**.
3. The **engine** is delivered on its own cadence — so the engine that *rejects* the old spelling reached **everybody**.
4. The resulting mixed tree (new engine, old packs) fails the self-test on `pack-manifests`, and `deliveryDecision` parks a failing tree's PR rather than merging it.
5. **That parked PR is the one that would have carried the new spelling.**

The fix could never arrive by the route that delivers fixes.

## Why nobody noticed

The work item reports success while the delivery is parked. TLDR's `core/update` closed **`outcome:done`** at 00:14:23Z with `Prework did this run's work; no agent was needed` — while its PR sat open, labelled `needs-human`, saying the tree failed its self-test. Five days of green-looking runs.

That reporting gap is arguably the more serious half: a converge that delivers nothing must not close `outcome:done`. Related to #892, but this is the agentless prework path, not agent discretion.

Also worth noting #926 already recorded the symptom — "HelloWorldFlutterApp and gRatio have no `pattern-rules.mjs` in their mount… Both last moved 2026-08-12" — without it being recognised as fleet-wide. It was: those two just showed it more visibly.

## The actual fix

Three candidates, not yet chosen:

1. **Deliver packs and engine atomically.** The mount is replaced wholesale by `engine-update.mjs` already; the pack half opting out via `packVersions` is what splits them. Simplest statement of the invariant: a member's packs are never older than its engine.
2. **Bump a pack's version whenever its `declared-checks.json` changes** — enforceable as a check (the file's hash vs. the declared version), but it relies on every future author remembering the rule the check then catches.
3. **Make the self-test's delivery gate distinguish "the tree I am delivering is broken" from "the tree I am replacing was already broken."** Parking on the latter is what makes the deadlock permanent — the gate refuses to deliver the fix *because the thing being fixed is broken*.

(1) and (3) are complementary, and (3) is the one that makes any future instance of this class recoverable rather than terminal. My inclination is (1) as the invariant plus (3) as the backstop, but this is a delivery-semantics change across the fleet and wants an explicit decision.

## Standing rule this instance confirms

> Tightening a contract that member-owned files must satisfy — first ask what carries it across the fleet. If the answer is "nothing", accept the legacy shape until a carrier exists.

The vocabulary rename tightened exactly such a contract. The answer to "what carries it" was *nothing*, and it was not asked.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/939","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","comments":1,"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-17T00:22:59Z","updated_at":"2026-08-17T10:11:31Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

[{"id":5314706390,"body":"## Correction: the scope is three repos, not the whole fleet

The body of this issue overstates the blast radius. Re-measured at 10:15Z:

| repo | `instructions.md` | `wake` input | declares `chrome-extension-release` |
|---|---|---|---|
| TLDR | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ (was blocked; unblocked by hand today) |
| CrosswordChat | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ **blocked** |
| GoogleCalendarEventCreator | ✅¹ | ❌ | ✅ **blocked** |
| LaughCounter, Sheepdog, EdFringeNow, VascularColoring, ShoutsAndWhispers, ClaudiniteCanary | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ — converged normally overnight |

¹ hand-written earlier, not delivered by a converge.

**Only members declaring `chrome-extension-release` were affected** — that is the pack whose `declared-checks.json` changed spelling without a version bump. Everyone else was never blocked and picked up #907/#925/#936 on their own anchors between 02:00Z and 06:00Z.

### How I got it wrong

At 00:20Z every member did show no `instructions.md` and `ref: 631a067f`, and I read that as fleet-wide freeze. But #907 had merged only hours before, so most members were simply **pre-anchor**, not stuck — they converged on schedule overnight.

The stale `ref` looked like corroboration. It isn't: this project's own rule says a held stamp makes a converging mount look weeks old, so `ref` cannot distinguish "frozen" from "fine". I used a signal already known to be unreliable to generalise from one genuinely-broken member (TLDR) to all of them, instead of re-measuring after the anchors passed.

The lesson worth keeping: **one confirmed broken member is evidence about that member.** Establishing that a fault is fleet-wide needs the fleet measured at a time when a healthy member would have moved.

### What is unchanged

The defect and its severity for affected members are exactly as described. The asymmetry is real, the deadlock is genuinely self-sustaining, and it will recur for *any* pack whose `declared-checks.json` changes without a version bump — the next one may hit a pack every member declares. The three fixes proposed in the body still stand, and #950 (the `outcome:done`-on-a-parked-PR reporting gap) is what let this run for days unseen, whatever the count.

3	description: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
4	---
5	
6	# Extract lessons from a conversation
7	
8	The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
9	taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
10	dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
11	what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.
12	
13	The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
14	surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
15	re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.
16	
17	## The goal
18	
19	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
20	waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
21	cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
22	a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.
23	
24	## Where the conversation comes from
25	
26	- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
27	  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
28	  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
29	  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
30	- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
31	  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.
32	
33	**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
34	when a session is done enough to mine.
35	
36	## What to look for — the friction signals
37	
38	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
39	necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
40	
41	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
42	
43	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
44	building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
45	answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
46	
47	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
48	user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
49	a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
50	the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
51	correctly **without the round-trip**.
52	
53	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
54	
55	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
56	that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
57	something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
58	convention and had it corrected in review.
59	
60	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
61	so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
62	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
63	first, not after a detour.
64	
65	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
66	
67	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
68	padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
69	hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.
70	
71	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
72	and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
73	(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
74	only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
75	was already optimal.
76	
77	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
78	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
79	the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
80	a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
81	loss of quality.
82	
83	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
84	
85	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
86	checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
87	fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
88	fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
89	relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
90	recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
91	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.
92	
93	## Two passes per log, and the second one may overturn the first
94	
95	A captured log gets a **fresh pass** within a day of capture and a **final hindsight pass** just before
96	retention deletes it, against the corpus as it stands by then. The hindsight pass is a real re-read, not a
97	formality: a friction signal that looked situational the first time may have recurred since, and a lesson
98	landed since may have made a keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes.
99	
100	## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it
101	
102	For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
103	(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
104	nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):
105	
106	- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
107	- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
108	  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.
109	
110	**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
111	beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
112	**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
113	deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
114	silence it replaced.

# Extract lessons from a conversation

The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two passes per log, and the second one may overturn the first

A captured log gets a **fresh pass** within a day of capture and a **final hindsight pass** just before
retention deletes it, against the corpus as it stands by then. The hindsight pass is a real re-read, not a
formality: a friction signal that looked situational the first time may have recurred since, and a lesson
landed since may have made a keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns

{"number":924,"title":"A losing claimant's own comment bumps updated_at, so contention postpones the leash reclaim it depends on","body":"Split out of #922 at the owner's direction — a latent issue the strike does **not** fix.

The tick's executing-leash reclaim keys on the item's activity clock, which is GitHub's `updated_at`. Every claim attempt posts a comment, and a comment bumps `updated_at` — including the attempt of an executor that goes on to *lose* the arbitration and walk away.

So on an item nobody is actually working, each losing claimant resets the clock the reclaim is counting down. The busier the queue, the more executors arrive, the further the recovery is pushed out. Under a `labeled`-event executor plus an hourly drain, an item can be re-touched often enough that the leash never elapses.

This is what made the observed stall on canon #860 ~10h rather than the ~1h the leash nominally promises: the failed claims kept the item looking alive.

#922 removes the *cause* of those repeated losing claims, so the common case goes away with it. What stays is the general property: whenever an executor genuinely dies mid-claim, any later claim attempt on that item defers its recovery. Contention postpones the mechanism that exists precisely to recover from failure.

Worth considering:
- read the last **heartbeat/claim by the current holder** as the activity clock, rather than the item's `updated_at` — the heartbeat work in #883 already introduces a per-holder liveness signal, which is the natural carrier;
- or have a losing claimant not write to the item at all, which needs a claim protocol that reads before it writes (a bigger change, and it trades away the property that makes the current one correct under a stale snapshot).

Not urgent — the failure needs a dead executor *and* ongoing contention on the same item — but it should not be discovered a second time from a stall.


The canon home runs the same engine from its repo root, where there is no `.claudinite/shared/` and the shared packs are `packs/`. So `changedPacks` is permanently empty here, and every precondition reading it is blind in the one repo whose canon moves every day:

- `core/update` loses the "a pack moved" arm of its overdue gate.

The two-root form the local pack's own rule prescribes:

```js
/^(?:\.claudinite\/shared\/)?packs\/([^/]+)\/.+/
```

A local pack (`.claudinite/local/packs/…`, `.claudinite/local_packs/…`) matches neither root, which is the intent.

28:`growth-extract` is the whole capture stage, and it runs **three skills** in order:
29-
30-1. [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) over the window's commits, merged
31-   PRs and issue discussion;
32:2. [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) over the logs captured
33-   from working sessions (plus the retention prune);
34-3. [prose-to-checks](skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md) over the prose **that run just wrote**, to see
35-   whether any of it upgrades to a check before the PR opens.
36-
37-Everything lands in **one** PR, delivered to land where the repo's delivery settings allow
38-(`engine/scheduler/deliver-pr.md`). The two extraction halves used to be two tasks firing in
39-the same nightly slot against the same local packs; they share the lesson bar, the promotion ladder
40-and the dedup surface ([extracting-lessons.md](extracting-lessons.md)), so the split bought nothing
41-and cost a second opus dispatch, a second PR, and two runs deduping against a corpus the other was
42-concurrently writing.
43-
44-The third step is why the standing `prose-to-checks-sweep` is **weekly**: fresh prose is already
45-offered a conversion the night it is written, so what the sweep sees is a backlog that moves on a
46-weekly clock.
47-
48-A member that wants the local stages without contributing lessons upstream **opts out of
49-promotion** on its own entry — `{ "id": "grow_with_claudinite", "config": { "promote": false } }`
50-— and the central promote stage skips it (absent or `true` = participate).

52:## The conversation lifecycle — capture in-session, extract in the daily task, retention
53-
54-The pack also owns **extraction from working sessions**, replacing the old in-session post-merge
55:lessons pass. Capture and extraction split by what each needs: **capture** needs the live session
56-transcript, so it runs in-session (at merge, and again when the session ends); **extraction** only
57-reads the already-pushed logs, so it is the conversation half of the ordinary `growth-extract`
58-scheduled task — the logs branch is *in the repo*, so reading it, committing lessons to local packs,
59-and pruning are plain local git on the working tree; only posting the summary on the issue uses the
60-GitHub MCP tools.
61-
62-1. **Capture — a step in the merge-to-main skill** (in-session, where the transcript lives).
63-   Right after a merge lands:
64:   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
65:   (in the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`).
66-   Deterministic, seconds; it bundles the session transcript (sidechains inline, timestamp
67-   order), **scrubs enumeration-first** (every value the environment holds — `process.env`
68-   minus a short named allowlist of structural values, plus known credential stores — is
69-   redacted wherever it appears, with credential-shape patterns as the backstop; a secret the
70-   session itself transformed is beyond any static scrub, and push protection is the last
71:   net), and pushes one file per **capture event** onto the orphan **`conversation-logs`**
72-   branch: `<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`, commits marked `[skip ci]`.
73:   **Delta-aware, keyed on the session id:** every capture pushes only the entries after this
74:   session's previous capture, whatever event produced it, so any two events chain into
75-   disjoint files and a zero delta pushes nothing at all. Double-writing is therefore safe by
76-   construction, not by coordination — the property [`session-end.mjs`](session-end.mjs) relies
77-   on, so `pack.test.mjs` pins it directly.
78-   The branch is a **work queue, not an archive** — never merged; tips are cheap in shallow
79-   session clones and retention keeps them bounded.
80-1. **Capture — again, when the session ends** ([session-end.mjs](session-end.mjs), invoked by the
81:   engine's SessionEnd hook runner for every active pack that ships one). Same capture, with
82-   `--issue 0`: **`0` means "no associated issue"**, and the filename shape stays byte-identical
83-   on purpose — the retention prune, the `conversationLogs` signal and the extract's filename
84-   parse all already accept it, whereas a *new* shape would be invisible to the prune and become
85:   immortal on the branch. This event is what captures the sessions that never merge (a review, an
86-   investigation, a session that ended in a question) and the post-merge **tail** of the ones that
87-   do. **Best effort:** a container reclaimed by timeout never fires it, so nothing depends on it
88-   having run — every firing enriches the record, every miss leaves exactly the merge-only
89-   behaviour. An `issue-0` log has no issue for the extract to post its exchange
90-   summary on; nothing else about its lifecycle differs.
91:   **Unattended sessions capture through the same step, deliberately not through the hook.** A
92-   scheduled task's executor session ends by having its container reclaimed, which is exactly
93-   the ending no `SessionEnd` fires on — so the executor runs the engine's runner itself as its
94-   last step and names its dispatch issue in `CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE`, which this step uses in
95-   place of `0`. Those logs therefore file under the task that ran (the dispatch issue's title
96-   names `pack/task`), and the work no human watched becomes as countable as the work one did.
97-2. **Fresh pass — the conversation half of [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md)**
98-   (precondition: a substantive merge, or a log actually past retention so the age-based prune still
99-   runs on a quiet repo; local git on the repo's working tree, MCP only for the issue comment). It
100-   applies the [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) skill (the
101-   friction signals and the measured efficiency analysis, computable from the log's timestamps and
102-   token usage) over [extracting-lessons.md](extracting-lessons.md)'s shared bar, routes keepers into
103-   the member's local packs, and posts on the worked issue, for each rule that landed, a
104-   **200-word-max** summary of the slice of conversation that caused it — the dialogue itself is
105-   never pasted there, it is far too verbose for an issue —
106-   **extraction is the only path to permanence**: a log that yields no rule gets no comment,
107-   and its conversation is gone once retention deletes it (a deliberate owner call).
108-3. **Final pass and deletion** — once a log ages past `config.retention_days`, the same task
109-   re-reads it with ~a week of hindsight (the rethink window), then deletes it (the age-based
110-   precondition arm guarantees the prune runs even on a repo gone quiet). Every log gets exactly two
111:   judgment passes. **Unset retention = the prune deletes nothing** (capture-only, fail-safe).
112-
113-No adoption question over it — `retention_days` stays unset (hidden) by default, which is
114:fail-safe (capture-only). A project that wants the prune active sets `config.retention_days`
115-itself (10 is the recommended floor); nothing else to schedule, since extraction rides the
116-fleet's one daily run like the other growth tasks.

119-
120-Mounting a skill only puts its name and one-line description into the session prompt; whether the
121-model ever **loads** it is discretion, and nothing recorded it. So the promotion ladder's

124-looked exactly like a genuinely activity-scoped one.
125-
126-The [usage-fold](tasks/usage-fold/task.md) task closes that loop — daily, agentless, seconds. It
127:counts skill loads **and their denominators** (captures, merges, sessions, user messages, user
