content.text:
## Part A — commits with non-obvious message content

- **3f1fb10 (#970)**: "Duplicating the sweep's verdict inside the unit suite reports a rule violation as a broken test, one step before the sweep that says it properly." Candidate lesson: a unit test that re-derives a repo-wide sweep's own verdict is redundant and mis-files a policy violation as a test failure — assert the runner *answers* (exit code / prints), never re-implement the rule it enforces.
- **ca20111 (#958)**: "A rule a check enforces is a copy on the check's clock. Cut." — when promoting/rewriting pack prose, drop any RULES.md bullet whose content a blocking/advisory check already fully covers; state it once, in whichever medium is load-bearing.
- **0180b6d (#963)**: Two callouts beyond the title — "Asked what happens to a repo carrying the old format, the honest answer needs a test rather than a claim" (a legacy-data-compat question gets proven with a see-it-fail test, not asserted), and "names the one change this format cannot absorb: renaming a counter... a rename keeps both spellings or takes the loss knowingly" (a versioned format's docs should state its own blind spot explicitly).
- All other 11 commits: nothing to add beyond their one-line summaries — see PRs #971, #969, #966, #965, #953, #962, #950, #956, #957, #949, #938 respectively.

## Part B — touched PRs

- **#977** (open, clean, 0 review comments): no durable lesson — body itself already names the drift class ("two spellings of one protocol in two trees") which duplicates the existing canon rule on that.
- **#941** (open, clean, 0 review comments): the body's own bug find — `delivered.issue` was populated by two workers but rendered by neither dispatch path, so a hand-off channel silently dropped data — is a real bug but codebase-specific; no generalizable lesson beyond "test that a struct field you add is actually consumed on every path," which existing test-discipline rules already cover.
- **#975** (open, clean, 0 review comments): the "One thing I assumed" note (interpreting an ambiguous owner comment about an "annoying" repeated line, stating the assumption rather than asking) is a live instance of the already-standing AskUserQuestion-default rule — no new lesson.

## Part C — touched issues

- **#976, #972, #964**: no comments (or design-only) — no discussion lesson.
- **#974** (1 comment): candidate lesson — a slot-era parameter channel silently returns `{}` under the new queue dispatch rather than erroring, so a safety knob (e.g. `DRY_RUN`) reads as accepted but is dead, defaulting the operation to its *most dangerous* mode (live, unscoped) with no complaint. Worth generalizing: a silently-dropped parameter is worse than a missing one — audit that a parameter channel's producer and consumer still agree after an interface migration.
- **#940** (2 comments): routine design-record narrowing by owner review; no new durable lesson beyond what #941/#964 already carry.
- **#801** (15 comments, large tracking issue): confirms the already-canonized "flip changed a contract, callers weren't swept" class (already in local RULES.md) — no new lesson there. But one self-correction is a fresh nuance: "I enumerated the fleet from what I already believed its membership to be, rather than from what the enforcer would enumerate at runtime" and "[the ref stamp] misled me... one confirmed broken member is evidence about that member [only]; establishing a fault is fleet-wide needs the fleet measured at a time when a healthy member would have moved." attachment.content:
- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: How to order the phases of an implementation or migration plan so nothing stalls mid-run — front-load the out-of-band setup, collapse the review gates into one stacked-PR pass, leave only executable steps — and how to keep its tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use when writing or reviewing a migration plan or a phased implementation plan, and when working through one's tracking issue.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.

- 2026-08-17T2208Z--issue-939--101a4a70-11d3-5c74-acf1-100cb9480276.jsonl
- 2026-08-17T2221Z--issue-939--101a4a70-11d3-5c74-acf1-100cb9480276.jsonl
- 2026-08-17T2238Z--issue-939--101a4a70-11d3-5c74-acf1-100cb9480276.jsonl

These are JSONL transcripts (one JSON object per line: user/assistant messages, tool_use, tool_result, each carrying a timestamp and token usage). They are DELTAS — each file holds only the entries added since that session's previous capture, so read all three in order, they are NOT redundant with each other. This is a DIFFERENT session than other issue-939 captures happening in parallel (different session id), so treat it independently.

Since these can be large, don't necessarily cat the whole file into your context blindly — you can use tools like `jq`, `grep`, `wc -l`, or Python to inspect structure first (e.g. `git show origin/conversation-logs:"<path>" | python3 -c "import sys,json; ..."` to extract just message roles/text/timestamps and tool_use/tool_result pairs with their timestamps), then read the interesting parts in full.

## What to look for (friction signals)

1. **Misunderstandings**: a clarifying round-trip, the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant..."), the agent building the wrong thing and reworking it, an AskUserQuestion whose answer was an obvious default in hindsight.
2. **Suboptimal agent actions**: backtracking, redundant/repeated work, re-running a command that already failed for a knowable reason, reaching for a heavy tool where a light one fit, reinventing something the codebase already provided, missing an existing convention corrected in review.
3. **Long wall-time waits — MEASURE them from real timestamps**: independent ops run serially with no dependency, a padded fixed sleep, a process waited out after its result was already in hand, blind long polling, re-running an already-green check. Compute actual wall-clock deltas between timestamps (in seconds/minutes), don't estimate.

A lesson only counts if it's durable/reusable/generalizable beyond this one session — not a one-off. This repo (Claudinite) is a system of packs/checks/skills giving AI coding agents durable working rules; landed lessons get written into `.claudinite/local/packs/{claudinite,canon-curation}/RULES.md`.

The repo's local pack RULES.md already contains extensive lessons about: AskUserQuestion costing ~170s median (spend it only on irreversible forks), Monitor/curl being proxy-blind for GitHub CI in this sandbox (read check runs via the GitHub MCP tool instead), git remote prune after squash-merge, rebase not merge to re-sync a moved main, restoring via git checkout not .bak files, capturing test-suite output to a file and grepping it instead of re-running, replying to every claim in an owner comment's first reply, converging an unattended run's outcome as the very next action, and many more (see the full RULES.md — it's extensive, so lean toward reporting anything genuinely new rather than assuming everything is covered).

Note: issue #939 was itself about "Manual tasks refused their own forced items, so both fleet levers were dead" (PR #971) — a scheduler bug investigation/fix, later revisited. This later session (101a4a70, evening of Aug 17) is likely a follow-up investigation or a different angle on the same issue.

## Output

For each of the 3 files, report: file name, whether it yielded a durable candidate lesson (or "nothing durable"), and if yes: the lesson in one sentence, a short supporting quote/citation, and (for wall-time findings) the measured number. Keep total response under 700 words.

import json

for fname in ["f1.jsonl","f2.jsonl","f3.jsonl"]:
    print("="*20, fname, "="*20)
    with open(fname) as f:
        lines = [json.loads(l) for l in f if l.strip()]

    # print roles and timestamps
    for i,e in enumerate(lines):
        t = e.get("timestamp","")
        typ = e.get("type", e.get("role",""))
        msg = e.get("message", {})
        role = msg.get("role","") if isinstance(msg,dict) else ""
        content = msg.get("content","") if isinstance(msg,dict) else ""
        summary = ""
        if isinstance(content, str):
            summary = content[:100].replace("\n"," ")
        elif isinstance(content, list):
            parts=[]
            for c in content:
                if isinstance(c,dict):
                    if c.get("type")=="text":
                        parts.append("TEXT:"+c.get("text","")[:80].replace("\n"," "))
                    elif c.get("type")=="tool_use":
                        parts.append("TOOL_USE:"+c.get("name","")+" "+json.dumps(c.get("input",{}))[:80])
                    elif c.get("type")=="tool_result":
                        cc = c.get("content","")
                        if isinstance(cc,list):
                            cc = " ".join([x.get("text","")[:60] for x in cc if isinstance(x,dict)])
                        summary_r = str(cc)[:80].replace("\n"," ")
                        parts.append("TOOL_RESULT:"+summary_r)
            summary = " | ".join(parts)
        print(f"[{i}] {t} {typ}/{role}: {summary[:200]}")
EOF

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/extract-from-conversations

# Extract lessons from a conversation

The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two passes per log, and the second one may overturn the first

A captured log gets a **fresh pass** within a day of capture and a **final hindsight pass** just before
retention deletes it, against the corpus as it stands by then. The hindsight pass is a real re-read, not a
formality: a friction signal that looked situational the first time may have recurred since, and a lesson
landed since may have made a keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/extract-from-conversations

# Extract lessons from a conversation

The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two passes per log, and the second one may overturn the first

A captured log gets a **fresh pass** within a day of capture and a **final hindsight pass** just before
retention deletes it, against the corpus as it stands by then. The hindsight pass is a real re-read, not a
formality: a friction signal that looked situational the first time may have recurred since, and a lesson
landed since may have made a keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/extract-from-conversations

# Extract lessons from a conversation

The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two passes per log, and the second one may overturn the first

A captured log gets a **fresh pass** within a day of capture and a **final hindsight pass** just before
retention deletes it, against the corpus as it stands by then. The hindsight pass is a real re-read, not a
formality: a friction signal that looked situational the first time may have recurred since, and a lesson
landed since may have made a keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

## Session summary

This log captures a `canon-curation/growth-promote` run (issue #870): scanning 8 members' local packs, deduping against the canon, and landing ~20 lessons across 9 canon files as PR #949. Most of the session was efficient parallel grep/read reconnaissance. Two friction points stood out; only one is durable and new.

**Not new (already covered):** the agent cut its working branch from local `main` without first `git fetch && reset --hard origin/main` (already the documented rule), discovered it was 34 commits stale, and had to stash, resync, and re-verify ~6 files it had checked on the stale branch — a ~2-minute self-inflicted detour that the existing "Syncing local main" rule would have prevented had it been followed.

**Durable finding — new:** Before pushing, the agent ran `check_the_world.mjs` (both `--changed` and full) and treated it as sufficient pre-push verification, then pushed and opened PR #949. CI failed: `packs-tests/rule-index.test.mjs` — a test `check_the_world.mjs` does not run — asserts every pack's `README.md` carries a hand-maintained per-rule row (name, severity, reason, exact word count) matching its `RULES.md`, plus a corpus-wide tally in `packs/README.md` (rule count + total words). The agent had edited/added bullets in `basics`, `core`, `headless-browser`, `git-github-advanced`, `scheduled-tasks.md`, `extracting-lessons.md`, and `unattended-agents` `RULES.md`/`SKILL.md` files without touching any README index, so the drift check failed on the merge-blocking `test-and-conformance` job.

Diagnosis cost real time: `get_job_logs` with `tail_lines: 3000` overflowed the tool's token cap ("224,603 characters... exceeds maximum allowed tokens"), forcing a fallback grep of the persisted spill file to find `not ok 1605 - each pack README indexes its RULES.md rules...`. Fixing meant hand-reconciling word counts and rule-name-length limits (a rule-index row name must stay ≤8 words) across four README files, then re-running the *actual* full suite for the first time (`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`, 1893 tests, ~76s, all green) before re-pushing.

**Measured cost:** CI failure surfaced 13:37:17Z; fix committed and pushed 13:43:41Z — a ~6.5-minute diagnose-and-fix detour, plus ~85s of blind-sleep CI polling (13:43:55→13:45:38) before merge. Running the ~76-second full suite proactively (as was in fact required, and was cheap once done) would have caught this before the first push at zero net cost, at the price of the 6.5-minute round trip actually paid.

**Lesson (one sentence):** Editing or adding a rule to any pack's `RULES.md`/skill prose must update that pack's `README.md` rule-index row (name ≤8 words, exact word count) and `packs/README.md`'s corpus-wide tally in the same change, and `check_the_world.mjs` passing is not evidence of this — only `node --test packs-tests/rule-index.test.mjs` (or the full suite) catches drift there.

**Citation:** CI log — `not ok 1605 - each pack README indexes its RULES.md rules, in order, with their word counts`; agent's own diagnosis: "No auto-generator — the README rule-index tables are hand-maintained."

**Suggested landing spot:** `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/RULES.md`, near the existing "Adding or changing a check — update the pack's catalog row" bullet (that one covers checks; this is its rule/prose counterpart, currently absent).

## Summary of findings across the 3 capture files

**File 1 — `2026-08-17T2208Z...jsonl`** (build+merge PR #965, `pack-version-bumped` check)
Nothing durable. Clean see-it-fail cycle (write rule → write test → flip a condition to watch it fail → revert → wire into pack → full suite → PR → check-runs → squash-merge → sync `main`). All matches conventions already in RULES.md.

**File 2 — `2026-08-17T2221Z...jsonl`** — two new candidate lessons.

1. **A scratch "probe" commit swept up an unrelated real edit, then got discarded with it.** The agent had already edited `.github/workflows/ci.yml` for real, then created `tmp-ci-probe`, ran `git commit -qam "probe: ..."` (which committed *all* modified files, including the pending `ci.yml` edit) to deliberately trigger `task-lifecycle`, and after confirming the red, ran `git checkout -q main && git branch -qD tmp-ci-probe` — destroying the `ci.yml` edit along with the probe. It noticed the loss and re-applied the edit (`git checkout -q -B claude/pack-version-validation-0rrjfk origin/main` then re-editing `ci.yml`).
   Quote: *"The probe commit swallowed my `ci.yml` edit and branch deletion dropped it — re-applying, this time on a proper branch first."* (22:12:24)
   Durable lesson: **before making a throwaway probe commit with `commit -am` on a scratch branch, stash or otherwise isolate any real in-progress edits — `-am` and a subsequent branch-delete will silently destroy unrelated pending work along with the probe.**

2. **Repeated blind fixed-length sleeps to wait out CI**, guessed rather than polled, because Monitor/curl are proxy-blind for GitHub checks in this sandbox (a rule already in RULES.md, so the *workaround itself* is the new signal): `node -e "setTimeout(...,75000)"` (22:14:55→22:16:13, 78s), then again `95000` (22:17:08→22:18:45, 97s), later in file 3 `100000` (22:22:37→22:24:19, 102s) and `110000` (22:26:28→22:28:21, 113s). Total ≈ 390s (6.5 min) of guessed, unconditioned sleeping across the session, each duration picked ad hoc rather than derived from a short retry loop against the already-available `mcp__github__pull_request_read(get_check_runs)` call.
   Durable lesson: **when the only CI-status channel is a per-call MCP tool (no proxy polling), loop that same call on a short interval (e.g. 15–20s) instead of guessing one long fixed sleep — the guessed durations here were consistently longer than needed and never adapted to actual completion time.**

**File 3 — `2026-08-17T2238Z...jsonl`** — one durable lesson, one reinforcing instance.

1. **The new CI-wiring guard test invoked the real work-scope runner against the actual live branch, so it failed for the wrong reason.** The user asked for a deliberate demonstration (probe PR #967 with an unbumped pack edit). CI went red — but at the "Unit tests" step, not the intended new "work-scope" CI step, because `engine-tests/ci-work-scope.test.mjs` itself called `check_the_work.mjs` in-process, and that call legitimately failed against the probe's own violating branch state, conflating the wiring guard with the live conformance check it was validating.
   Quote: *"My own guard test was the culprit — it re-runs the work sweep inside the unit suite, so a violating branch reds at the wrong layer. That test should assert the runner *works*, not that this branch is [clean]."* (22:26:02) — fixed by having the guard assert only that the runner *answers cleanly*, not that the current branch passes it.
   Durable lesson: **a CI-wiring/guard test that literally re-invokes the real command it's guarding, against the actual current branch, will fail whenever that branch happens to violate the real rule — conflating "is the CI step wired correctly" with "does this branch pass conformance." Guard tests for wiring should assert invocation shape/behavior in isolation, never live branch state.**

2. Reinforcing (not new): after reporting the red build with a paraphrase ("failed... not at a specific stage"), the user pushed back ("I'm not sure I understand... why do I care"), and the agent had to re-answer by quoting the actual printed test output verbatim. This is an instance of the already-captured "lead with the throwing call site, not a narrative" rule — worth noting only as reinforcement, not a new item.

## Findings

**File 1: `2026-08-17T1001Z--issue-939--...jsonl`** — durable candidate lesson found.

Diagnosing a fleet-wide outage from repo probes, the agent hit two compounding traps in one sequence (00:15:22–00:16:00Z): an unauthenticated `curl https://api.github.com/repos/$r/pulls...` loop across 9 repos got silently rate-limited and returned a uniform "(no open update PR)" for every repo — which read as a real answer, not a failure. The agent noticed the rate-limit itself ("The API probe is being rate-limited unauthenticated — let me check the mounts directly instead") but then fell back to a *second* probe (raw.githubusercontent.com mount files) that also came back identical across all 9 repos (`instructions=404 wake_input=0 stamped_ref=631a067f`), and from that uniformity concluded "**Every member is frozen** on the same stale ref." That claim was posted publicly and stood for ~10 hours until the 10:10Z re-check (see file 2) showed only 3 of 9 repos were actually stuck — the rest simply hadn't hit their nightly anchor yet, coincidentally sharing the same pre-update stamp. Lesson: an unauthenticated `api.github.com` list/probe call can be rate-limited into a clean-looking negative result across every target — check for rate-limit signals explicitly before trusting a uniform empty/negative sweep; and a uniform value across every member of a fleet is itself a signal to check *timing* (pre-anchor vs. actually-stuck) before generalizing to "fleet-wide," not confirmation that it's fleet-wide.

**File 2: `2026-08-17T2030Z--issue-939--...jsonl`** — same lesson as above resolves here (10:10:43Z: "I have to correct my previous message: **'the entire fleet is frozen' was wrong.**... What misled me: at 00:20Z every member genuinely showed no `instructions.md` and `ref: 631a067f`. But #907 had only merged hours earlier, so most were simply *pre-anchor*, not stuck.") — report this as the resolution half of the file-1 lesson, not a separate one.

Additionally, a second, distinct pattern: after already launching a background watcher (`until curl ... check-runs`) for a PR's CI, the agent still manually re-polled `mcp__github__pull_request_read{get_check_runs}` and the watcher's own output file in a tight loop instead of waiting for the completion notification — burning calls that returned identical "in_progress" data. In file 2 this ran ~20:29:54–20:30:40Z (5 `pull_request_read` calls + 2 wasted `Read`s on the unchanged watcher-output file in ~46s).

**File 3: `2026-08-17T2247Z--issue-974--...jsonl`** — durable candidate lesson found (the double-polling pattern, sharpest instance, with explicit self-correction).

The same launched-a-watcher-then-polled-anyway pattern recurs at 22:41:19–22:41:59Z: immediately after backgrounding `until curl .../check-runs ... do sleep 20; done`, the agent alternated `mcp__github__pull_request_read{get_check_runs}` and `Read` on the watcher's output file **4 times each** in 40 seconds, getting "Wasted call — file unchanged since your last Read" twice, before catching itself: "I'm burning calls polling — the watcher will wake me when CI lands, so I'll stop and merge then." Measured: 8 redundant polling calls in a 40-second window that a single background notification would have covered. This generalizes beyond this session: once a background watcher for an async completion (CI, a workflow dispatch) is running, don't also hand-poll the same signal through a second channel in a tight loop — wait for the task-notification, exactly as the harness's own "Wasted call" feedback (fired 5 times total across all three files) was already trying to signal.

### Durable lesson: placement churn from not front-loading "which distribution model" for new Claudinite capability

The agent built a Claudinite task dashboard and was told, across three separate follow-up turns, to relocate it entirely:

1. **Turn 1** (23:22): built it in `dev/tools/tasks-dashboard/` as a standalone local-run tool.
2. **Turn 2** (00:16): user corrected — "I don't run things locally... the dashboard should be in `engine/scheduler/dashboard` for any project to mount... I want an uber-dashboard in Sheepdog." Superseded — closing. Everything this PR added is now the `claudinite-dashboard` pack's job") since the pack's own scaffolding subsumed it.

Each move required: `git mv`, import-path rewrites (including a missed backtick-template-literal import that broke tests silently until caught — `packs-tests/claudinite-dashboard/auth.test.mjs: Cannot find module`), test-path rewrites, README rewrites, and a fresh render/screenshot verification pass. The pack's own README even states the deciding fact in hindsight ("`.github/workflows/` is the one directory the nightly update can never push to... so a deploy workflow can only ever arrive by being seeded" — exactly what `packs/canary-probe` already demonstrates as the pattern for this).

This is distinct from the existing `file-placement` skill (which governs *where within a repo* a file sits by reference distance) — this is the higher-level "which distribution model" call, and getting it wrong costs a full move-and-rewrite cycle, observed three times in one session.

This is a **recurrence** of an already-documented rule (`Re-verifying a branch against a main that has moved — git rebase, never merge`), not new signal — but worth flagging that the rule as written didn't prevent the mistake in a live run; it was only caught after the fact by the existing check. - The rate-limit header parsing bug (`Number(null) === 0` misread as "zero remaining") is a textbook instance of the already-documented "unknown as zero" trap — confirms the existing rule's value, not new.

### Wall-time check

No agent-caused idle waiting was found. The large gaps in the log (33352s, 5862s, 2213s, 894s) are all user-absence periods between conversation turns (the user replying hours later), not the agent blocking on anything — no padded sleeps, no redundant polling, no serial-when-parallelizable operations detected.

## Session-by-session findings

### issue-955 (840e7941, 20:28Z capture)
**Durable candidate — borderline.** The agent first placed a Claude-Code-web-only setup script under the generic `engine/hooks/`, then the owner corrected: *"the engine/hooks/environment-setup-command.sh is relevant for the claude-code-web-users-support, not the engine. Please move it."* This forced a second full round of file moves, doc edits, and a rebase. This is a specific instance of the already-loaded `file-placement` principle (place by owning responsibility, not by mechanism the file happens to be wired through), so I'm not proposing a new standalone rule — flagging only because it cost a full correction round-trip and a forced rebase.

No new wall-time waste found beyond what's already covered (CI polling here was efficient — used the GitHub MCP tool directly).

### issue-961 (840e7941, 21:28Z capture — delta of the same session)
**Nothing new.** The `AskUserQuestion` about fleet-force policy was an appropriate irreversible-fork use, and the resulting rule refinement ("force delivery only when 'will it work on every repo?' is a live question") is already present verbatim in the current `claudinite/RULES.md`. Already landed, not a re-extraction target.

### issue-960 (aa68783a, 21:45Z capture)
Two genuinely new, durable, measured findings:

1. **Poll cadence with no backoff.** Waiting on PR #956's CI, the agent called `mcp__github__pull_request_read {get_check_runs}` on a **fixed ~5s cadence** with no backoff: 14 calls between `20:26:56` and `20:28:03` (**67 seconds, ~14 polls**) just to watch one run to completion. The existing rule only says *use the MCP tool instead of Monitor/curl* — it says nothing about polling interval. A rolling backoff (e.g., 15s → 30s) would cut this to ~3-4 calls for the same wait with no loss of responsiveness.

2. **Pushing to an already-open, bot-authored PR needs an explicit CI dispatch.** Twice in this session (at `21:38` and again at `21:43` after a rebase), pushing a new commit to the existing PR branch left `get_check_runs` returning `{"total_count":0}` for ~15-20s — GitHub's own recursion guard blocks `pull_request: synchronize` from firing for a GITHUB_TOKEN-authored push (confirmed by the CI file's own comment: *"a GITHUB_TOKEN-authored PR... never turns into a pull_request run"*). The agent correctly diagnosed this via `actions_list` and called `mcp__github__actions_run_trigger` (workflow_dispatch) both times, but only after first spending 2 failed `get_check_runs` polls. Worth stating as a proactive step: after pushing a **second-or-later** commit to an existing agent-authored PR, call `actions_run_trigger` immediately rather than waiting for CI to appear on its own.

Also noted but not proposing a rule: three background `sleep 100/60/130` commands were launched during this same CI wait and never actually gated anything (the agent kept polling directly regardless) — clutter, not wall-clock waste, since `run_in_background` didn't block.

### issue-959 (432a0c70, 22:18Z capture)
**Strong new architectural lesson.** The agent put a format module needed by two packs (`grow_with_claudinite`'s usage-fold and `sheepdog`'s fleet-usage) into `engine/`. The owner corrected: *"We can't ever have code that needs to be shared by two packs saved in 'engine'. That breaks the model... I don't want it to be a pack dependency because that would force bringing a whole lot of rules and behaviours that were not requested."* The agent's fix in two steps is the durable pattern:
- First check whether the "sharing" is even necessary — the real fix was noticing the fleet sweep never needed to *interpret* the member's format at all (self-describing rows: each file declares its own field vocabulary).
- For the one piece that genuinely was identical logic in two packs (a tiny generic JSON renderer), the owner rejected even a shared-file-with-drift-guard: *"Actually, why do you even need a drift guard? Just write the json. Don't overkill."* — outright duplication per pack, because cross-pack coupling (even a guarded one) violates pack independence, was preferred over the corpus's usual "prefer a shared constant + drift guard" convention.

This refines the existing shared-constant/drift-guard rule with a boundary condition it doesn't currently carry: **that convention applies within a pack or between a pack and the engine's own internals — never across two sibling packs**, where duplication is the correct default and `engine/` is never the escape valve.

### issue-968 (5e56f9e2, 22:35Z capture)
**Nothing new.** Clean, mechanical run (bumping 29 pack versions). The recurring `Skill: merge-to-main` → `Unknown skill` failure appeared again (4th occurrence across this whole batch) but is already covered by the existing "unmounted skill" rule; each occurrence just costs one failed tool call before falling back to reading the file directly, not worth a new rule.

## Summary of proposed new lessons
1. Cross-pack shared code never goes in `engine/`; first ask whether the two packs actually need to share logic at all (self-describing data can remove the need), and if genuine duplication is needed, prefer outright per-pack duplication over a shared-with-drift-guard module — pack independence overrides the usual anti-duplication convention (issue-959).
2. Pushing a subsequent commit to an already-open PR authored by the agent's own token won't auto-trigger `pull_request` CI (GitHub's recursion guard) — dispatch `actions_run_trigger` immediately after such a push rather than polling and discovering the gap (issue-960, confirmed twice, ~15-20s lost each time diagnosing it).
3. When polling `get_check_runs` for a CI wait, use a rolling backoff instead of a fixed ~5s cadence — measured 14 calls over 67s for one wait (issue-960).

1	# Claudinite — the canon's own non-portable working rules
2	
3	Lessons specific to working on the canon itself. Anything true for repos beyond this one belongs in
4	the shared canon under `packs/`/`skills/` instead. The `growth-extract` task appends here, each
5	lesson at the strongest mechanism available — a check where the rule is deterministic, else prose.
6	
7	## Standing owner decisions — settled, do not re-litigate
8	
9	- **Wanting a rule about what the `packs/` tree may reference** — declare and configure the
10	  `barriers` pack, extending it generically if a capability is missing. Never write standalone
11	  code that checks packs-tree segregation.
12	
13	- **Writing a `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md`** — the mechanism only. Status, phase tracking and
14	  remaining work live in the tracking issue; a phased plan in the sibling `MIGRATION.md`.
15	
16	- **Ending a session on unfinished work** — write the state into the tracking issue. The
17	  owner's opener is `continue work on #<n>`, so anything else is lost; never compose a hand-off
18	  prompt.
19	
20	- **Designing anything that spans repos** — split it: a self-contained per-repo half in the
21	  canon, the aggregation half as a Shepherd fleet task. No repo list exists anywhere in canon
22	  code; Shepherd enumerates members at runtime. A derived fleet artifact lands there as a daily
23	  auto-merged PR of a `GENERATED` file, never a commit to its `main`.
24	
25	- **Choosing a value right for nearly every project** — keep it in the pack's own code: ask
26	  nothing at adoption, write nothing into the member's config. Read config as optional — an
27	  unset key means the default, never "misconfigured".
28	
29	- **Needing a member to flip a platform setting or hold a wider credential** — last resort:
30	  per-repo manual work reliably does not happen, and the capability then dies silently in every
31	  repo nobody configured. Prefer the route that works with the Action's own `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and
32	  neutralise a blocking platform behaviour's *effect* rather than asking for the platform to be
33	  reconfigured. Where nothing weaker can work (`FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`), name the exact scope and
34	  have the automation report when it is missing rather than degrade silently.
35	
36	- **Landing a change to what members receive** — force delivery in the same session only when
37	  *"will it work on every repo?"* is a live question: the answer turns on how members differ —
38	  engine flow, a contract their own files must satisfy, a stub or workflow, a migration record, a
39	  new config key. Then drive Shepherd's `fleet-baseline` with `follow`, report per member unasked,
40	  and attach the repos that verification needs rather than offering to; a dispatch is not a result,
41	  and 204 means queued. Where the change is uniform by construction — prose, a doc, a move of
42	  something nothing executes from the mount — the nightly converge *is* the delivery, and forcing
43	  buys noise rather than assurance.
44	
45	- **Retiring a field, option or module** — `@deprecated` on its definition, plus a comment at
46	  each sanctioned holdout's declaration site saying why it still carries the field. Never a
47	  bespoke conformance check for a deprecation. Keep the contract validating the lingering field.
48	
49	- **Wanting a `.claudinite-checks.json` entry's config validated** — that is a real JSON Schema
50	  the file points at with `$schema`, checked by ordinary tooling. Never a coded per-pack
51	  validation vocabulary or a bespoke `configSchema` type system on the manifest — built and
52	  reverted in #919 ("That's why we have schemas").
53	
54	## Working with the owner and the session's tools
55	
56	- **Answering "why did it fail?"** — lead with the throwing call site: `file:line`, the
57	  function, and which side enforced it. A correct narrative that never names the line reads as
58	  unanswered.
59	
60	- **Reaching for `AskUserQuestion`** — it blocks for minutes (~170s median), so spend it only
61	  on a fork you cannot take back. Anything answerable from the instruction, the tree, or a
62	  reversible default: answer it, act, and say what you assumed. Never re-post a question that was
63	  declined — take its recommended default, or open the question up.
64	
65	- **Being asked to generalise something, or to review it** — land the conversions or action
66	  points it unlocks in the same change. A capability ships with the caller that exercises it; an
67	  analysis ships with the first of its recommendations applied.
68	
69	- **Calling anything on `Claude_Code_Remote`** — one call per intent, ever. Each costs
70	  minutes, and a call that returns nothing has *not* failed — the retry has run to 81% of a
71	  session's tool wall-clock. For "is it green yet" read the check status directly; to read a
72	  public sibling repo, `git clone --depth 1` (~2s), since `add_repo` attaches nothing the git
73	  proxy doesn't already serve.
74	
75	- **Waiting for something to happen** — the guard must name the condition awaited (a run's
76	  status, a file's arrival, a deadline), with no trailing padded `sleep`. A guard you wouldn't
77	  write as the *whole* test means you are sleeping and calling it polling. **Exception: GitHub
78	  CI/PR check status is not this repo's case for `Monitor` or a `curl`/shell poll loop** — this
79	  sandbox proxy-blocks `api.github.com`, so both silently report "still running" until they time
80	  out (measured ~26 minutes lost across two PRs waiting past an already-green check, #880). Read
81	  the head sha's check runs with the GitHub MCP tool instead.
82	
83	- **Replying to an owner comment that raises more than one claim** — answer **every** claim in
84	  that first reply, including the one you intend to push back on. A claim left silently
85	  unaddressed, even when the rest of the reply is right, just makes the owner re-raise it later
86	  (#864: a placement objection went unanswered for 55 minutes before the owner repeated it).
87	
88	## Authoring packs, prose and checks
89	
90	- **Writing a paragraph that explains how a mechanism works** — not into a pack's `RULES.md`,
91	  which every session in every declaring repo pays for. Behaviour belongs in the module header and
92	  the pack `README.md`; the test is whether an agent could act differently for having read it.
93	
94	- **Having a deferred direction, blocked proposal or status to record** — put it in `docs/`
95	  and point at it from the issue or PR, not from a pack file: `docs/` is outside the vendor set.
96	
97	- **Naming a new canon pack** — kebab-case, named for the surface it serves rather than the
98	  first feature you are building for it. The directory name is the pack's public id, spelled in
99	  every member's declaration, so another casing costs a fleet-wide rename. `grow_with_claudinite`
100	  is grandfathered. (convertible → prose-to-checks)
101	
102	- **Looking for a skill and not finding it in `.claude/skills/`** — read
103	  `packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` out of the tracked tree. Mounting filters on the *literal*
104	  declaration and the home doesn't declare `git-github`, so an unmounted skill says nothing about
105	  whether its procedure applies.
106	
107	- **Adding or changing a check** — update the pack's catalog row, and re-run the suite against
108	  current `main` before merging: a whole-tree aggregate is judged post-merge, so a branch's own green
109	  never covers it. Never transcribe a corpus-wide total into a doc — `packs/README.md` states how to
110	  count checks and rules instead of quoting a number, so every pack change no longer edits it.
111	  (portable → `merge-to-main`)
112	
113	- **Writing a check's `fix` text** — name only remedies that match the enforced severity;
114	  sessions follow the words, not the `severity` field. An advisory finding's remedies are act on
115	  it or leave it, never a config-acceptance escape.
116	
117	- **Declaring a check, or adding a key to the vocabulary** — name the key so the declaration
118	  reads alone to someone who hasn't read the design doc (`scanFiles`, `matchLines`,
119	  `relevantWhen`): if it needs a comment to be read, it needs a better name. Declarations live in
120	  `packs/<pack>/declared-checks.json`, which cannot hold one, and borrow nothing from prose — no
121	  `description`, no `doc`; the line the agent reads is `failureMessage`.
122	
123	## The engine, the mount and what reaches members

125	- **Writing a path, regex or command against the mount** — write the two-root form: the
126	  `.claudinite/(shared|local)/` prefix optional in a pattern, and a probe for
127	  `.claudinite/shared/` falling back to the repo root. The home runs the same code from the repo
128	  root, so a mount-shaped path works fleet-wide and fails on exactly this repo — where it
129	  surfaces last.
130	
131	- **Adding a module under `packs/`** — keep it import-light, and start work after evaluation
132	  completes (`check(…).catch(…)`), never in a top-level `await`. Discovery imports every
133	  `pack.mjs` and `checks.mjs` before activation is consulted, so a module that is also a CLI entry
134	  point is re-imported mid-evaluation and Node exits 13 having run nothing.
135	  `pack-discovery-entry-await` enforces the await half only.
136	
137	- **Tightening a contract that member-owned files must satisfy** — first ask what carries it
138	  across the fleet. Vendoring refreshes `.claudinite/shared/` only and a migration record moves
139	  paths, not schemas — so if the answer is "nothing", accept the legacy shape in
140	  `normalizeManifest` until a carrier exists. Never let a stale declaration degrade to *fewer
141	  checks running* rather than a failure.
142	
143	- **Extending what a copied stub reads** — make the new config key optional, fail the run when
144	  it is declared-but-unset, and let declaring it trigger a staleness check (`build_vars` /
145	  `release-workflows` is the shape). Stubs are copied into a member's `.github/` once and never
146	  re-copied, so a new key is silently dead in every repo holding the old copy.
147	
148	- **Writing a migration record that needs engine behaviour newer than itself** — have
149	  `appliesTo` probe the member's own mount for that capability, by content rather than version,
150	  and stay inert until it reads back; an unreadable mount must read as "not capable". The record
151	  comes from a fresh canon clone but the worker executing it is the member's vendored one, so
152	  otherwise the converge fails, the mount never advances, and the fix can never arrive.
153	
154	- **Changing an export in `updates/*`** — empty it, never remove it. Fielded workers are stale
155	  callers of instantly-current flow modules, so a removal wedges every member permanently on its
156	  next run. Keep it callable, say at its definition that this is why, and pin the surface with a
157	  test carrying an expiry — the canary rehearsal cannot catch this class, since it drives the
158	  worker this ref ships. Retire it by reading the field: the condition is that no member's
159	  *vendored* worker calls it.
160	
161	- **Changing a vendored stub** — edit the canon's own `.github/workflows/` copy in the same
162	  commit and diff the two whole files. The canon has no converge, so its copy drifts invisibly
163	  until it is a permission denial in production.
164	
165	- **Excluding files from the vendor set by pattern** — whitelist any operational file that
166	  matches by path, and pin it with a test against the real canon tree, not only a fixture. The
167	  nightly refresh re-runs the computation from canon HEAD, so a bug there is the one canon
168	  regression that is not self-healing. Assert that the **whole containing directory** vendors,
169	  not just the one file that broke — a test re-asserting only the known-missing file needs a
170	  fresh edit for the next file added there; one that walks the real directory doesn't (#907).
171	
172	- **Retiring or reshaping a protocol the engine exposes** (a dispatch input, a stub's declared
173	  interface) — sweep for callers **outside this repo**, not just what greps locally. `FORCE_TASKS`'s
174	  replacement broke Shepherd's only caller because the migration enumerated this repo's own
175	  callers and missed the cross-repo one (#929); two independently-maintained stub copies at the
176	  same path declaring different input names is the same failure from the other side (#801, #907)
177	  — the two spellings *are* the protocol, and they live in different trees.
178	
179	- **Branching on the result of an API write in fleet machinery** — read its status, not just
180	  the body: a body-only destructure turns a 403 into a plausible object and the run still logs
181	  `ok`. Judge the fleet by members' stamps, never by run conclusions — the stamp is the only
182	  artifact that moves when delivery actually worked.
183	
184	- **Writing generated content into a size-capped GitHub API field** (an issue or PR body) —
185	  budget it explicitly, in two tiers: an always-complete compact summary plus best-effort detail
186	  rationed to a byte budget with an explicit omitted-count, never a single unbounded write that
187	  can 422 outright at the ~64KB cap. `growth-dedup`'s brief rendered 350KB against that limit and
188	  would have failed the run at its first step.
189	
190	- **Adding a fleet task** — fail loudly on a Context target it cannot reach rather than
191	  proceeding on a partial list, and treat a member as un-adopted until the routine's repo scope
192	  names it. The target list is enumerated over `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` while the grant is hand-typed
193	  UI config no Action can read; the drift *completes*, filing a report that reads as a full sweep.
194	
195	- **Spawning a child process from a worker** — pass an explicit `cwd`, resolved to a root that
196	  cannot vanish (`--root`, then `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, then `cwd`). The converge deletes the tree
197	  its own prework runs inside, so children die at `process.cwd()` before doing anything. Keep
198	  "could not run" distinguishable from "had nothing to run": a crash sharing a benign outcome code
199	  is unobservable.
200	
201	- **Diagnosing a member's maintenance PR that won't land** — `unstable` beside a green sweep
202	  is a parked `action_required` run, not a missing repo setting. Read the member's raw
203	  `.claudinite-checks.json` and the head sha's `pull_request` runs; propose a platform-settings
204	  change only as a conclusion, never as a diagnosis.
205	
206	- **Judging whether a member is fresh** — read its `ref` (or `engineVersion` /
207	  `packVersions`), never `claudinite.updated` alone: a held stamp pins `updated` behind a pending
208	  note, so a mount converging hourly can look a week stale.
209	
210	## Scheduled tasks
211	
212	- **Choosing a task's cadence** — take it from how often the signal actually moves. A
213	  precondition reading `sharedMount` fires nearly every night and spends an opus dispatch on it;
214	  where the work isn't latency-sensitive, daily buys noise, not freshness, and a weekly run still
215	  sees all 7 days because `windowStart` widens to the widest due task's period.
216	
217	- **Writing a task's precondition** — gate on the objects' own movement in the window (a
218	  `touched` list, a tip-commit date the collector actually carries), never on standing state,
219	  which is true forever once true. A signal true most days — a substantive `main` move — may
220	  only *widen* an already-triggered run. The gate is not the scope: where a verdict is relative to
221	  the rest of the set, newness gates and the full set stays the scope. (portable →
222	  `core/scheduled-tasks.md`)
223	
224	- **Writing a task whose output is a regenerated file** — land it through
225	  `engine/scheduler/deliver-generated.mjs` and read its prior state from the fetched base, not
226	  local HEAD. Every due task in a run shares one checkout, so a worker that checks out a branch or
227	  leaves an index behind hands the next task a tree it did not expect. (`basics/baselining` is the
228	  deliberate exception.)
229	
230	- **Wanting to exercise a task Action-side** — invoke its worker directly, or move the slot
231	  hour and wait for the cron. Dueness is stateless, so a `workflow_dispatch` outside the slot's
232	  window succeeds, prints `- no tasks due`, and does nothing — looking exactly like a healthy
233	  run.
234	
235	- **Converging an unattended run** — do the final label/comment/close sequence as the run's very

242

244	
245	- **Testing a change to a task's triggering** — drive the real `planRun` from a deliberately
246	  non-due slot. The due list is computed before any precondition runs, so a test starting inside
247	  that gate proves only "works once evaluated".

281	
282	- **Surveying whether something exists in the tree** — a code-search hit is evidence; a
283	  code-search miss is not. Survey by reading each file.
284	
285	## Editing, branching and merging here
286	
287	- **Editing a repo's JSON config** — patch it as anchored text; never re-serialize. A
288	  round-trip rewrites what it wasn't asked to (`ensure_ascii` escapes, indent, key order, trailing
289	  newline) while nothing fails and tests stay green. (portable → `repo-text-sweeps`)
290	
291	- **Returning to a branch that waited** — after `git fetch`, re-verify the *premise*, unasked:
292	  read what the new commits did to the surface you are changing and say whether the problem is
293	  still there and what survives. This repo auto-merges its own PRs on top of migrations that
294	  retire whole directories, so a branch can rebase cleanly, stay green, and no longer be the
295	  change to make.
296	
297	- **Re-verifying a branch against a `main` that has moved** — `git rebase origin/main`, never
298	  `git merge origin/main`. A merge commit trips the blocking squash-merge-history check and costs
299	  a full rebase, a discarded CI run, and a fresh wait — paid twice in one evening on #880.
300	
301	- **After a PR lands by squash-merge** — `git remote prune origin` before touching that branch
302	  again. GitHub deletes the head ref on squash-merge here, so a stale local tracking ref makes git

304	  phantom local work (#922).
305	
306	- **Re-applying your edit onto a moved `main`** — re-read the fetched file, apply the same
307	  anchored edit, and confirm the stat shows insertions only. A pack's `RULES.md` is append-only
308	  and written several times a day, so restoring a whole-file copy deletes those lessons and
309	  nothing goes red.
310	
311	- **Syncing local `main`** — `git fetch origin main && git reset --hard origin/main`,
312	  unconditionally. The clones are shallow, so `git pull` finds no common ancestor and reports the
313	  stale local ref as carrying unique commits; nothing of value is ever on this repo's local
314	  `main`. (portable → `git-github`)
315	
316	- **Merging in a session that also has a consumer repo in its sources** — resolve the merge
317	  skill by *target repo*, not by which skill matched first. The consumer's skill wins on name and
318	  is followed to the letter, silently skipping the canon-only steps — repeatedly the post-merge
319	  conversation capture (`node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), which is
320	  part of the merge, not an optional epilogue.
321	
322	- **Having work that completes or corrects an open PR** — put it on that PR's branch. A
323	  dispatch prompt's designated branch routes work, not review; splitting gives the owner two gates
324	  for one decision and invites approving half.
325	
326	- **Wanting to combine two PRs** — update the one you're keeping and close the other. Never
327	  push one's branch onto the other's base: GitHub marks a PR merged as soon as its head is
328	  reachable from its base, and a later `state: closed` is a no-op. Check the API's `merged` field
329	  before reporting.
330	
331	- **Being asked "should no X decide this?"** — it questions whether the decision exists at
332	  all; never answer it by relocating the knob one rung out. Ask who would ever set it differently
333	  and why that can't be read off the structure — a single structural answer means delete the
334	  field and document the exception where it lives.
335	
336	- **Facing a retry across a call whose outcome you cannot observe** — check whether declining
337	  to retry removes the uncertainty before building dedup or arbitration machinery to manage it. A
338	  timeout is exactly the case where you cannot know the first call did nothing.
